options.text: The liquid must receive exactly 100t joules, irrespective of the vessel's heat capacity.
The liquid receives 100/t joules because power is energy divided by time.
The electrical energy supplied is 100t joules, but the liquid receives less if some energy warms the vessel and probe.
The electrical energy supplied is 100+t joules.

explanation: Electrical energy supplied is Q_{electrical}=Pt=100t mathrm J. Some of this energy may heat the vessel and probe, so the liquid's share can be smaller. Option A incorrectly equates electrical input with the liquid's heat gain without accounting for the apparatus.

title: Finding the water equivalent from an experimental diagram
question: A copper calorimeter and its stirrer have a combined heat capacity equivalent to 20 g of water. The calorimeter initially contains 100 g of water. Both are at 20°mathrm C, and a hot body is added. For a small temperature rise of 5°mathrm C, how much heat is absorbed by the water, calorimeter and stirrer together? Use c_=4.2 J/(g,°C).
diagramSvg:
<svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 145" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">
    <path d="M60 35 H260 L245 112 H75 Z" fill="#CBD5E1" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5"/>
    <path d="M69 65 H251 L243 105 H77 Z" fill="#38BDF8" fill-opacity=".6"/>
    <path d="M160 15 V82 M146 82 H174" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/>
    <rect x="130" y="75" width="60" height="22" fill="#D97706" stroke="currentColor"/>
    <text x="160" y="10" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Stirrer</text>
    <text x="160" y="55" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">100 g water</text>
    <text x="160" y="130" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Calorimeter + stirrer: water equivalent 20 g</text>
  </svg>

options.text: 2100 mathrm J
2520 mathrm J
420 mathrm J
210 mathrm J

explanation:
The total water equivalent is 100+20=120 mathrm g.


Q=mcΔ T
=120×4.2×5
=2520 mathrm J


Option A omits the calorimeter and stirrer, using only the 100 g of water.

title: Identifying the correct boiling plateau
question: A pure liquid is heated at constant pressure. Its temperature rises to 100°mathrm C, remains constant while vigorous boiling continues, and then rises again after all the liquid has vaporised and the vapour is still heated. Which statement correctly explains the horizontal section at 100°mathrm C?
diagramSvg:
<svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 160" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">
    <path d="M42 18 V130 H298" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" fill="none"/>
    <path d="M42 118 L96 80 L215 80 L277 32" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2.5" fill="none"/>
    <path d="M42 80 H298" stroke="currentColor" stroke-opacity=".25" stroke-dasharray="4 4"/>
    <text x="8" y="18" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">T (°C)</text><text x="8" y="84" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">100</text>
    <text x="57" y="105" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Liquid</text><text x="127" y="70" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Boiling</text><text x="231" y="48" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Steam</text>
    <text x="166" y="149" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Time</text>
  </svg>

options.text: The liquid's temperature stays constant while energy supplies the latent heat of vaporisation.
The liquid stops absorbing energy because its temperature is fixed.
The specific heat capacity of the liquid becomes infinite, so no phase change occurs.
The liquid's temperature must rise continuously because the heater supplies energy continuously.

explanation: At the boiling point, supplied heat is used to convert liquid into vapour. The temperature remains constant during the phase change at a fixed pressure. Option D confuses energy supplied with temperature rise and ignores latent heat.

title: Interpreting experimental readings for specific heat capacity
question: Two equal masses of different substances, P and Q, are heated separately using identical constant-power heaters. The following readings are recorded. Which conclusion follows from the readings?

font-size="12" font-weight="normal" fill="#334155">Final temperature</text><text x="170" y="135" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="normal" fill="#334155">45°C</text><text x="310" y="135" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="normal" fill="#334155">65°C</text><text x="30" y="167" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="normal" fill="#334155">Heating time</text><text x="170" y="167" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="normal" fill="#334155">100 s</text><text x="310" y="167" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="normal" fill="#334155">100 s</text></svg>

options.text: c_P=c_Q, because both receive heat for the same duration.
c_P=2c_Q, because P has half the temperature rise.
c_Q=2c_P, because Q reaches the higher final temperature.
c_P=2c_Q, because equal heater power and time provide equal heat, while P's temperature rise is half that of Q.

explanation:
1. Both heaters supply equal energy because Q=Pt, with equal P and t.
2. Both masses are equal.
3. P's temperature rise is 45-25=20°mathrm C, while Q's is 65-25=40°mathrm C.
4. Since c=Q/(mΔ T), the smaller temperature rise corresponds to the larger specific heat capacity.

Thus, c_P/c_Q=40/20=2. Option C mistakes a higher final temperature for a higher specific heat capacity.

title: Interpreting a complete heating curve
question: The graph shows a pure substance being heated steadily from ice below 0°mathrm C until all the water has become steam above 100°mathrm C, at normal atmospheric pressure. Schematic heating curve: AB, BC, CD, DE and EF represent successive heating and phase-change stages. Which interpretation of the five successive portions is correct?

<svg viewBox="0 0 460 200" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="background:#f8fafc; border-radius:8px; border:1px solid #cbd5e1; font-family:system-ui, sans-serif;">

options.text: AB: melting; BC: warming of ice; CD: boiling; DE: warming of water; EF: condensation.
AB: warming of ice; BC: melting; CD: warming of water; DE: boiling; EF: warming of steam.
AB: warming of ice; BC: melting with rising temperature; CD: warming of water; DE: boiling with falling temperature; EF: warming of steam.
AB: warming of ice; BC: boiling; CD: warming of water; DE: melting; EF: warming of steam.

explanation:
1. On AB, the ice temperature rises towards 0°mathrm C.
2. On BC, ice melts at constant temperature.
3. On CD, liquid water warms towards 100°mathrm C.
4. On DE, water boils at constant temperature.
5. On EF, steam becomes hotter than 100°mathrm C.

The trap in C is that temperature does not rise during melting or remain constant only briefly during boiling; the idealised phase-change portions are flat.

title: Comparing the specific heat capacities of two liquids
question: Equal masses of liquids X and Y are heated separately by identical heaters of constant power. Both start at 20°mathrm C. After 4 minutes, X reaches 60°mathrm C, whereas Y reaches 40°mathrm C. Which conclusion is justified?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 205" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M42 18 V160 H300" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" fill="none" /><path d="M42 120 H300 M42 80 H300 M42 40 H300" stroke="currentColor" stroke-opacity=".18" stroke-dasharray="4 4" /><text x="8" y="18" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">T (°C)</text><text x="22" y="163" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">20</text><text x="22" y="123" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">30</text><text x="22" y="83" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">40</text><text x="22" y="43" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">50</text><path d="M42 120 L282 0" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2.5" fill="none" /><path d="M42 120 L282 80" stroke="#0284C7" stroke-width="2.5" fill="none" /><text x="238" y="20" font-size="12" fill="#D97706">X</text><text x="238" y="75" font-size="12" fill="#0284C7">Y</text><text x="146" y="181" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Time (min)</text><text x="40" y="175" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">0</text><text x="272" y="175" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">4</text><text x="42" y="199" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Schematic; stated readings govern</text></svg>

options.text: c_X=2c_Y, because X has twice the temperature rise for the same supplied heat.
c_Y=2c_X, because Y's temperature rise is smaller.
Both liquids have equal specific heat capacities because the heaters are identical.
The heat capacity of X is twice that of Y, regardless of their masses.

explanation: For equal masses receiving equal heat, Q=mcΔ T, so specific heat capacity is inversely proportional to the temperature rise. The rises are 40°mathrm C and 20°mathrm C, respectively. Therefore c_Y=2c_X. Option D confuses heat capacity with specific heat capacity and does not state the required mass relationship.

title: Heat capacity versus specific heat capacity
question: Two blocks made of the same material are heated separately. Block P has a mass of 200 g and block Q has a mass of 500 g. Which statement must be correct, assuming both blocks are at the same temperature?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 120" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="30" y="30" width="95" height="42" rx="4" fill="#94A3B8" stroke="currentColor" /><rect x="185" y="30" width="105" height="42" rx="4" fill="#64748B" stroke="currentColor" /><text x="77" y="48" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">P</text><text x="77" y="63" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">200 g</text><text x="237" y="48" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">Q</text><text x="237" y="63" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">500 g</text><path d="M77 75 V88 M237 75 V88" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" /><text x="160" y="109" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Same material</text></svg>

options.text: Q has 2.5 times the specific heat capacity of P.
P has 2.5 times the heat capacity of Q.
Q has 2.5 times the heat capacity of P, but their specific heat capacities are equal.
Both their heat capacities and specific heat capacities are equal.

explanation: Heat capacity C=mc. For the same material, c is the same, so C_Q/C_P=500/200=2.5. Specific heat capacity is an intensive property and does not increase merely because more material is present.

title: The role of the calorimeter's polished surface
question: Two otherwise identical calorimeters contain equal masses of hot water at the same temperature. One has a polished outer surface and the other has a dull, blackened outer surface. Why is the polished calorimeter generally preferred for calorimetry experiments?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 145" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="35" y="35" width="95" height="78" rx="7" fill="#CBD5E1" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" /><rect x="45" y="60" width="75" height="43" fill="#38BDF8" fill-opacity=".7" /><rect x="190" y="35" width="95" height="78" rx="7" fill="#334155" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" /><rect x="200" y="60" width="75" height="43" fill="#38BDF8" fill-opacity=".7" /><text x="82" y="22" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Polished</text><text x="237" y="22" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Blackened</text><path d="M24 52 l-10 -6 M24 67 l-10 0 M141 52 l10 -6 M141 67 l10 0" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="1.5" /><path d="M178 52 l-10 -6 M178 67 l-10 0 M297 52 l10 -6 M297 67 l10 0" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="1.5" /><text x="160" y="135" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Equal initial conditions</text></svg>

options.text: It reflects more thermal radiation and reduces radiative heat exchange with the surroundings.
It prevents all conduction through the calorimeter walls.
It increases the specific heat capacity of copper.
It makes the calorimeter absorb no heat from the contents.

explanation: A polished surface is a poor emitter and absorber of thermal radiation, helping reduce radiative exchange. It does not eliminate conduction or make the calorimeter's heat capacity zero.

title: Heat absorbed by the calorimeter
question: A copper calorimeter contains water. The thermometer and stirrer are both immersed in the water, while the calorimeter is surrounded by an insulating jacket. When hot water is mixed with colder water inside this apparatus, which energy balance is the most complete?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 190" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="50" y="28" width="220" height="145" rx="9" fill="#94A3B8" fill-opacity=".18" stroke="currentColor" stroke-dasharray="5 4" stroke-width="1.5" /><path d="M82 62 L238 62 L224 151 L96 151 Z" fill="#CBD5E1" stroke="#64748B" stroke-width="2" /><path d="M92 90 L228 90 L220 145 L100 145 Z" fill="#38BDF8" fill-opacity=".6" /><path d="M157 36 V111" stroke="#DC2626" stroke-width="2.5" /><circle cx="157" cy="113" r="5" fill="#DC2626" /><path d="M190 55 V112 M180 112 H200" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" /><path d="M238 62 L280 48" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1" /><text x="280" y="44" text-anchor="end" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Copper vessel</text><path d="M157 80 L120 48" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1" /><text x="118" y="43" text-anchor="end" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Thermometer</text><path d="M190 88 L229 37" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1" /><text x="230" y="32" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Stirrer</text><text x="160" y="184" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Insulated jacket</text></svg>

options.text: Heat lost by hot water = heat gained by cold water only.
Heat lost by hot water = heat gained by the copper vessel only.
Heat lost by hot water = heat gained by cold water minus heat gained by the vessel.
Heat lost by hot water = heat gained by cold water + calorimeter + stirrer, provided other losses are negligible.

explanation: The vessel and stirrer also warm up and absorb heat. Neglecting their contributions generally gives an incorrect final temperature or an incorrect calculated specific heat capacity.

title: Identifying the correct method-of-mixtures arrangement
question: A hot metal block is transferred from a heated bath into a calorimeter containing cooler water. The metal is weighed before transfer, and the water and calorimeter temperatures are measured before and after mixing. Which procedure most reduces systematic error in determining the metal's specific heat capacity?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 170" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="15" y="54" width="95" height="72" rx="5" fill="#93C5FD" fill-opacity=".35" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" /><path d="M25 84 H100 V119 H25 Z" fill="#38BDF8" fill-opacity=".6" /><rect x="48" y="67" width="34" height="25" fill="#DC2626" stroke="currentColor" /><text x="62" y="42" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Hot bath</text><path d="M112 76 C137 51 151 51 171 76" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2" fill="none" /><path d="M165 68 L173 77 L161 79" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2" fill="none" /><path d="M187 54 H292 L282 126 H197 Z" fill="#CBD5E1" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" /><path d="M194 84 H286 L281 120 H200 Z" fill="#38BDF8" fill-opacity=".6" /><rect x="224" y="91" width="32" height="20" fill="#DC2626" stroke="currentColor" /><path d="M244 22 V85" stroke="#DC2626" stroke-width="2" /><circle cx="244" cy="87" r="4" fill="#DC2626" /><text x="238" y="42" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Thermometer</text><text x="239" y="145" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Calorimeter + water</text><text x="160" y="163" text-anchor="middle" font-size="9" fill="currentColor">Transfer rapidly; minimise heat exchange</text></svg>

options.text: Allow the hot block to cool in air before placing it in the calorimeter.
Dry the block and transfer it rapidly, while accounting for the calorimeter's heat capacity.
Leave the calorimeter uncovered and omit its heat capacity.
Measure only the final temperature because the initial temperatures are unnecessary.

explanation: Water adhering to the block can add unaccounted heat and mass, while cooling during transfer lowers its actual initial temperature. Including the calorimeter's heat absorption is also essential. Option A deliberately increases the temperature uncertainty.

title: Determining specific heat capacity from a temperature–time graph
question: Equal masses of substances P and Q are heated by identical constant-power heaters. Their temperature–time graphs are straight lines, with P having the steeper slope. What follows from the graph?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 175" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M42 18 V137 H298" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" fill="none" /><path d="M42 118 L270 25" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2.5" fill="none" /><path d="M42 118 L270 79" stroke="#0284C7" stroke-width="2.5" fill="none" /><text x="274" y="25" font-size="12" fill="#D97706">P</text><text x="274" y="79" font-size="12" fill="#0284C7">Q</text><text x="8" y="18" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">T</text><text x="166" y="157" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Time</text><text x="50" y="132" font-size="9" fill="currentColor">Same start</text><text x="160" y="173" text-anchor="middle" font-size="9" fill="currentColor">Equal masses; equal heater power</text></svg>

options.text: c_P>c_Q, because P heats more quickly.
c_P=c_Q, because both graphs are straight lines.
c_P<c_Q, because P's temperature rises faster for the same heat supplied per unit time.
The graph proves that P absorbs latent heat.

explanation: Since P_{heater}=mc,(Δ T / Δ t), equal power and mass imply cpropto1/slope. P's steeper slope therefore means a smaller specific heat capacity. Straightness alone does not prove equal specific heat capacities.

title: Interpreting a horizontal segment on a cooling curve
question: A pure liquid cools at normal atmospheric pressure. The temperature falls from 80°mathrm C to 50°mathrm C, remains at 50°mathrm C for a period, and then falls further. Which statement best explains the horizontal section?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 170" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M40 18 V137 H298" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" fill="none" /><path d="M42 30 L105 75 L190 75 L275 122" stroke="#0284C7" stroke-width="2.5" fill="none" /><path d="M42 75 H298" stroke="currentColor" stroke-opacity=".2" stroke-dasharray="4 4" /><text x="9" y="22" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">T</text><text x="166" y="157" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Time</text><text x="200" y="66" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">50°C</text><text x="64" y="47" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Liquid</text><text x="128" y="65" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Phase change</text><text x="215" y="110" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Solid</text></svg>

options.text: The substance is freezing, and energy is released as latent heat while its temperature remains constant.
The substance has stopped transferring energy to the surroundings.
The substance's specific heat capacity has become zero.
The substance is still cooling at a constant rate but the thermometer cannot detect it.

explanation: During freezing, latent heat is released while the liquid–solid mixture remains at the freezing point. Energy continues to leave the substance; the temperature does not fall until the phase change is complete.

title: Why water is useful in a hot-water bottle
question: Two identical bottles contain equal masses of water and another liquid, both initially at 80°mathrm C. Assume equal heat losses over a short interval and that the other liquid has a lower specific heat capacity than water. After each bottle loses the same quantity of heat, which is correct?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 130" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="52" y="36" width="75" height="66" rx="12" fill="#38BDF8" fill-opacity=".5" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" /><rect x="69" y="23" width="41" height="15" rx="3" fill="#94A3B8" stroke="currentColor" /><rect x="190" y="36" width="75" height="66" rx="12" fill="#F59E0B" fill-opacity=".35" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" /><rect x="207" y="23" width="41" height="15" rx="3" fill="#94A3B8" stroke="currentColor" /><text x="89" y="62" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="currentColor">Water</text><text x="89" y="79" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">80°C</text><text x="227" y="62" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Other liquid</text><text x="227" y="79" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">80°C</text><text x="160" y="120" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Equal masses; equal heat loss</text></svg>

options.text: Both liquids have the same temperature drop because their initial temperatures were equal.
Water experiences the larger temperature drop because it stores more energy.
The other liquid must release less heat because its specific heat capacity is lower.
Water experiences the smaller temperature drop because its larger specific heat capacity gives it a larger heat capacity for equal mass.

explanation: From Q=mcΔ T, for fixed Q and m, the temperature drop is inversely proportional to c. Water's high specific heat capacity makes it useful for storing thermal energy. Equal initial temperatures do not imply equal temperature changes.

title: Identifying a faulty calorimetry reading
question: A calorimeter initially contains 100 mathrm g of water at 20°mathrm C. A hot metal block is added. The measured final temperature is 30°mathrm C, but the experimenter forgets to include the calorimeter's own heat capacity in the calculation. What is the likely effect on the calculated specific heat capacity of the metal?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 155" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M68 38 H252 L238 124 H82 Z" fill="#CBD5E1" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" /><path d="M77 67 H243 L235 117 H85 Z" fill="#38BDF8" fill-opacity=".55" /><rect x="138" y="74" width="42" height="28" fill="#D97706" stroke="currentColor" /><path d="M158 17 V70" stroke="#DC2626" stroke-width="2.5" /><circle cx="158" cy="72" r="4" fill="#DC2626" /><text x="160" y="13" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Thermometer</text><text x="160" y="145" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Metal + water + copper vessel</text></svg>

options.text: It is necessarily correct because the calorimeter is in thermal equilibrium with the water.
It is underestimated because some heat lost by the metal also warms the calorimeter, but the calculation attributes the heat gained only to water.
It is overestimated because the calorimeter releases energy during mixing.
It becomes zero because the calorimeter and water have the same final temperature.

explanation: The metal's heat loss equals the heat gained by the water plus that gained by the calorimeter. Omitting the latter underestimates the metal's heat loss in the calculation. For the same metal mass and initial-to-final temperature drop, this produces an underestimated specific heat capacity.

title: Land breeze and sea breeze
question: Two panels represent daytime and nighttime conditions at a coast. During the day, land is hotter than the sea; at night, land is cooler than the sea. Which explanation correctly connects the diagrams to the specific heat capacity of water?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 130" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="10" y="28" width="145" height="67" fill="#BAE6FD" stroke="currentColor" stroke-opacity=".4" /><rect x="165" y="28" width="145" height="67" fill="#FDE68A" stroke="currentColor" stroke-opacity=".4" /><path d="M10 70 H155 V95 H10 Z" fill="#38BDF8" /><path d="M165 65 H310 V95 H165 Z" fill="#D97706" fill-opacity=".45" /><text x="82" y="17" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Sea</text><text x="237" y="17" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Land</text><path d="M126 53 H51" stroke="#0284C7" stroke-width="2.5" /><path d="M58 47 L50 53 L58 59" stroke="#0284C7" stroke-width="2.5" fill="none" /><text x="160" y="115" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Day: sea breeze blows sea → land</text><text x="160" y="127" text-anchor="middle" font-size="9" fill="currentColor">Land heats faster than water</text></svg>

options.text: Water has a lower specific heat capacity than land, so it changes temperature more slowly.
Water and land have identical specific heat capacities, but sunlight heats the land for longer.
Water has a higher specific heat capacity, so its temperature changes more slowly than land's for comparable heat transfer per unit mass.
The breeze is caused only by water evaporating, not by unequal heating.

explanation:
correctly connects the diagrams to the specific heat capacity of water?

A) Water has a lower specific heat capacity than land, so it changes temperature more slowly.

B) Water and land have identical specific heat capacities, but sunlight heats the land for longer.

C) Water has a higher specific heat capacity, so its temperature changes more slowly than land's for comparable heat transfer per unit mass.

D) The breeze is caused only by water evaporating, not by unequal heating.

**Correct Answer: C**

**Reason:** Water's higher specific heat capacity means it warms and cools more slowly for the same heat transfer per unit mass. The resulting temperature difference between land and sea drives the breeze. Option A reverses the specific heat relationship.

title: Ice added to water: locating the energy requirement
question: A piece of ice at 0°mathrm C is placed in a calorimeter containing warm water. The process has two stages: the ice melts, and the meltwater then warms to the final equilibrium temperature. Which expression gives the total heat absorbed by m grams of ice at 0°mathrm C that completely melts and reaches T°mathrm C, where T>0?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 155" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="12" y="25" width="88" height="75" rx="5" fill="#BAE6FD" stroke="currentColor" /><path d="M23 56 L40 43 L55 54 L45 69 L28 68 Z" fill="#E0F2FE" stroke="#0284C7" /><text x="56" y="17" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Ice at 0°C</text><path d="M105 61 H139" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" /><path d="M132 55 L140 61 L132 67" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" fill="none" /><rect x="145" y="25" width="70" height="75" rx="5" fill="#38BDF8" fill-opacity=".5" stroke="currentColor" /><text x="180" y="52" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Meltwater</text><text x="180" y="66" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">at 0°C</text><path d="M220 61 H250" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" /><path d="M243 55 L251 61 L243 67" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" fill="none" /><rect x="256" y="25" width="52" height="75" rx="5" fill="#38BDF8" fill-opacity=".5" stroke="currentColor" /><text x="282" y="50" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Water</text><text x="282" y="64" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">at T</text><text x="160" y="126" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Stage 1: melting</text><text x="160" y="141" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Stage 2: warming liquid water</text></svg>

options.text: Q=mL_f+mc_{water}T
Q=mc_{ice}T
Q=mL_f only, because melting fixes the temperature.
Q=mL_f+mc_{ice}T, using the specific heat capacity of ice for the liquid stage.

explanation: First, melting requires mL_f. Then the liquid water warms from 0°mathrm C to T°mathrm C, requiring mc_{water}T. Option D uses the wrong specific heat capacity for the second stage.

title: Steam passed into cold water
question: Steam at 100°mathrm C is passed through a delivery tube into water initially below 100°mathrm C. The steam condenses, and the resulting water cools to the final mixture temperature. Which heat contribution must be included when calculating the heat released by the steam after it enters the water?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 160" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="15" y="65" width="75" height="68" rx="5" fill="#CBD5E1" stroke="currentColor" /><path d="M22 89 H83 V126 H22 Z" fill="#38BDF8" fill-opacity=".5" /><path d="M25 72 C40 60 52 75 63 61 C72 52 82 60 87 54" stroke="#64748B" stroke-width="2" fill="none" /><text x="53" y="148" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Steam source</text><path d="M85 65 V45 H172 V75" stroke="#64748B" stroke-width="4" fill="none" /><path d="M85 65 V45 H172 V75" stroke="#F59E0B" stroke-width="1.5" fill="none" /><rect x="125" y="65" width="80" height="68" rx="5" fill="#CBD5E1" stroke="currentColor" /><path d="M132 91 H198 V126 H132 Z" fill="#38BDF8" fill-opacity=".55" /><path d="M172 75 V106" stroke="#F59E0B" stroke-width="2.5" /><circle cx="172" cy="110" r="4" fill="#F59E0B" /><text x="165" y="148" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Cold water</text><text x="235" y="43" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Steam at 100°C</text><path d="M231 48 L183 48" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1" /><text x="242" y="88" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Condenses</text><path d="M239 92 L190 105" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1" /></svg>

options.text: Only the heat required to raise the condensed water from 0°mathrm C.
Only the heat released when the steam condenses.
The heat released during condensation and the heat released when the condensed water cools from 100°mathrm C to the final temperature.
The heat absorbed by the steam to remain at 100°mathrm C.

explanation: Each gram of steam releases latent heat L_v on condensation and then releases additional sensible heat as the liquid cools. Thus, for m grams of steam ending at T_f°mathrm C, the released heat is mL_v+mc_{water}(100-T_f). Option B omits the cooling of the condensed water.

title: Comparing heating graphs for different masses
question: The same constant-power heater is used for two samples of the same liquid. Sample P has mass m, while sample Q has mass 2m. Both begin at the same temperature, and neither undergoes a change of state. If the graph slopes are s_P and s_Q, which relation is expected?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 170" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M42 18 V137 H298" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" fill="none" /><path d="M42 119 L270 25" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2.5" fill="none" /><path d="M42 119 L270 72" stroke="#0284C7" stroke-width="2.5" fill="none" /><text x="274" y="26" font-size="12" fill="#D97706">P (m)</text><text x="274" y="72" font-size="12" fill="#0284C7">Q (2m)</text><text x="8" y="18" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">T</text><text x="166" y="157" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Time</text><text x="160" y="173" text-anchor="middle" font-size="9" fill="currentColor">Same liquid; same heater power</text></svg>

options.text: s_Q=2s_P, because Q contains twice the material.
s_P=2s_Q, because doubling the mass halves the temperature rise per unit time.
s_P=s_Q, because the specific heat capacity is unchanged.
The slope ratio cannot be determined even when the heater power and substance are identical.

explanation: Since (dT / dt)=(P / mc), doubling the mass halves the slope. The specific heat capacity remains the same, but the total heat capacity doubles. Option C confuses a material property with the total heat capacity of the sample.

title: Reading heat supplied against temperature rise
question: A graph plots heat supplied Q on the vertical axis against temperature rise Δ T on the horizontal axis. The straight line for substance P is steeper than that for substance Q. Both samples have equal masses. What does the steeper line for P signify?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 165" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M42 18 V135 H298" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" fill="none" /><path d="M42 135 L110 35" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2.5" fill="none" /><path d="M42 135 L265 65" stroke="#0284C7" stroke-width="2.5" fill="none" /><text x="115" y="32" font-size="12" fill="#D97706">P</text><text x="270" y="64" font-size="12" fill="#0284C7">Q</text><text x="8" y="18" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Q (J)</text><text x="165" y="154" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">ΔT (°C)</text><text x="160" y="168" text-anchor="middle" font-size="9" fill="currentColor">Equal masses</text></svg>

options.text: P has a lower heat capacity because its temperature rises less.
P has a higher specific heat capacity only if its mass is greater.
The slope represents latent heat, even though the graph shows temperature rising.
P has a greater heat capacity and, for equal masses, a greater specific heat capacity.

explanation: The graph's slope is Q/Δ T=C, the heat capacity. For equal masses, c=C/m, so P also has the greater specific heat capacity. Latent heat is associated with a change of state at constant temperature, not this rising-temperature segment.
